intro: Real-world graphs are messy and unpredictable, but most trained models assume clean, stable data. The work splits into four directions: defending against attacks that deliberately corrupt graphs, handling structural changes that break models across domains, adapting to graphs where similar nodes are not connected together, and training across multiple graphs without centralizing data.

groups.label: Defending against graph attacks
writeup: Graph neural networks process information by passing messages along edges, which makes them sensitive when edges change. An attacker can add or remove edges to make a fraudulent node look normal, or to make the model misclassify benign nodes. The challenge is that an attacker with limited budget can cause outsized damage by exploiting the message-passing structure.

EvA develops a way to attack graphs more efficiently using evolutionary techniques. Instead of randomly trying edge changes, it finds the most damaging changes by simulating how the network would respond, then picks the edges that hurt prediction the most. This achieves much larger accuracy drops with far less computation and memory.

Text-Attributed Graph Learning and Resilience studies a different threat: graphs where nodes have text descriptions, not just features. The analysis reveals a hard tradeoff: if you make the model trust text more, it ignores the graph structure and becomes vulnerable to text-based attacks; if you trust structure more, text attacks don't work but structural attacks do. The paper shows that the text encoder (the system that converts text to numbers) matters because a weak encoder loses information, which means attacks that exploit text succeed faster. The paper proposes a balanced defense method that uses information from both text and structure, weighting them so neither one dominates.

BOCLOAK attacks bot-detection systems that use graphs to catch fake accounts. It uses optimal transport (a mathematical method for finding the best matching between two sets) to find which fake-account edges will look most natural and bypass detection, while using 99.80% less memory than previous attacks. Together, these papers show that attacks are more successful when they target the model's actual weak point—the place where it relies most heavily on one type of information—rather than randomly changing edges. This is why EvA's targeted approach and BOCLOAK's focused strategy both work better than broad attacks.

groups.label: Adapting when graph structure shifts
writeup: A graph model trained on one social network may fail completely on another, because the structure differs: one network is dense and tight, another is sparse with communities. The model learned to rely on message patterns that no longer exist. The challenge is learning representations that work even when the graph structure changes, without requiring labels in the new domain.

GP2F adapts pre-trained models to new graphs by learning how to combine multiple existing models in a way that respects the constraints of the new graph's topology. Instead of retraining from scratch, it fuses what existing models learned, weighted by which edges matter most in the new domain.

Alignment Across Domains studies this more broadly across 16 different domain shifts. It captures how features and structure link together at multiple scales (local neighbor patterns and longer-range connections), and learns to match the training domain and new domain by comparing these patterns without requiring labels on the new data. The approach aligns the patterns of features and edges between the old domain and the new domain—ensuring they have similar relationships in both places.

Progressive Graph Structure Adjustment directly modifies the graph structure during adaptation. When a model trained on a dense graph (homophilous, where similar nodes connect) encounters a sparse graph (heterophilous, where different types of nodes connect), the model fails. This paper gradually adjusts the graph structure by reweighting edges, keeping only the ones that matter for the current model, so the model can operate in the new regime. The point is that homophily is not a fixed property—it is relative to what the model has seen, so adjusting the edges adjusts what the model observes.

groups.label: Handling heterophilic graphs
writeup: Standard graph models assume similar nodes connect to each other (homophily). But many real graphs violate this: in disease networks, infected nodes connect to healthy ones; in recommendation graphs, users follow content they disagree with. When the graph is heterophilic, message-passing breaks because passing information from neighbors no longer means passing information from similar nodes.

Demystifying Common Beliefs in Graph Machine Learning breaks down heterophily into clearer pieces. Heterophily is not one issue but several: oversquashing (information bottlenecks in deep models), over-smoothing (all nodes become similar after many layers), and genuine node dissimilarity. The paper shows that these problems need different solutions, and that earlier papers mixed them together. By clarifying what problem you actually face, you can design a targeted fix.

Progressive Graph Structure Adjustment directly addresses the heterophily shift scenario. When test data comes from a heterophilic graph but the model trained on homophilous data, the model fails. Rather than retraining, the paper adjusts edge weights to create a homophilous subgraph that the pre-trained model can operate on, then adapts the model incrementally as the graph structure changes. This pragmatic approach works when the heterophily difference is large.

groups.label: Training across distributed graphs
writeup: In federated learning, data lives on separate devices and cannot be centralized due to privacy rules. For graphs, this is especially hard because message-passing requires neighbors, but neighbors may be on different devices. The challenge is training a model that works across all graphs without moving data to one place.

Temporal Graph Thumbnail handles graphs that change over time and are noisy (missing edges, spurious edges). Instead of processing the entire graph at every step, it builds a compact skeleton that captures the long-term evolution of the graph, then uses this skeleton for representation learning. This is efficient and reliable when the graph is partially missing or corrupted.

Homophily-Heterogeneity Gradient Surgery solves a specific federated learning problem: some clients have homophilous graphs (tight clusters) and others have heterophilous graphs (mixed types of neighbors). Standard federated averaging treats all clients equally, which causes the model to oscillate between solving for one type of graph and the other. This paper adjusts gradients during training to weight each client's update by whether their graph is homophilous or heterophilous, so the final model works for both types without extra data collection on clients.

SAGA handles multiview graph domain adaptation, where different views of the same graph (e.g., different types of relationships) have different amounts of shift. It learns which views are useful at each hop distance in the message-passing, adapting dynamically so that if a view is unreliable at distance 1, it down-weights that view but may use it at distance 2. This preserves information from all views while tuning trust based on what the data shows.
